title: Python Fundamentals for AI
summary: Python is the primary language of AI and machine learning because of its simple syntax and rich ecosystem of libraries. Today you learn the core building blocks: how to store data in variables, make decisions with if-statements, repeat work with loop
content:
# Python Fundamentals for AI ##### The line of code that cost a startup ₹2.8 lakh A two-person GenAI startup in Pune shipped a document-summarising tool in their first month. It worked beautifully in testing. Then a customer uploaded a 400-page compliance manual, and their script did this: ```python while chunks_remaining: summary = call_llm(next_chunk()) ``` `chunks_remaining` was set once, before the loop, and never updated. The loop never exited. It called an LLM API in a tight cycle for nineteen hours before anyone noticed the billing alert. ₹2,81,400. Neither founder was a bad engineer. They just did not yet have the reflex — the one that makes an experienced developer's eyes snag on a `while` whose condition nothing inside the loop can change. That reflex is what today builds. Everything glamorous in generative AI — retrieval pipelines, agents, fine-tuned models — is Python underneath. Variables holding API responses. Loops iterating over document chunks. Functions wrapping model calls. Dictionaries carrying the JSON that every LLM API speaks. If the fundamentals are shaky, the sophisticated parts are built on sand. So we start here, properly. ##### Why Python owns AI Python is not the fastest language. It is not the most elegant. It won AI for two reasons. **Readability.** Python code reads close to English, which matters enormously when the person writing it is a researcher or a domain expert rather than a career software engineer. Compare summing a list in Java versus `sum(numbers)`. **The ecosystem.** NumPy arrived in 2006 and gave Python fast numerical arrays backed by C. Everything stacked on top: pandas, scikit-learn, PyTorch, TensorFlow, Hugging Face Transformers, LangChain, LlamaIndex. Travis Oliphant's 2007 paper *Python for Scientific Computing* argued Python could be the glue language for science; two decades later, essentially every major AI lab writes Python. For you as a GenAI engineer, this means: the OpenAI SDK is Python. The Anthropic SDK is Python. ChromaDB, Pinecone, FAISS, sentence-transformers — Python. There is no path through this field that avoids it. ##### Variables and data types A variable is a name bound to a value. Python figures out the type for you. ```python model_name = "gpt-4o-mini" # str — text temperature = 0.7 # float — decimal number max_tokens = 512 # int — whole number stream_output = True # bool — True or False system_prompt = None # NoneType — deliberate absence print(type(temperature)) # ``` Those five types cover the overwhelming majority of what you will handle when talking to an LLM API. Two collection types complete the picture, and we will go deeper on Day 2: ```python stop_sequences = ["\n\n", "###"] # list — ordered, changeable request = { # dict — key → value lookup "model": model_name, "temperature": temperature, "max_tokens": max_tokens, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarise this."}], } ``` Look carefully at `request`. That is exactly the shape of a real LLM API call — a dictionary containing a list containing dictionaries. Getting comfortable with nested structures now pays off the first day you touch an API. **Naming matters more than beginners expect.** Use `snake_case`. Use names that say what the thing is: `retrieved_chunks`, not `rc` or `data2`. You will read your own code far more often than you write it. ##### Operators and expressions Arithmetic behaves as you would expect, with two operators worth calling out: ```python total_tokens = 1_847 # underscores are ignored — readability aid cost_per_1k = 0.15 # ₹ per 1,000 tokens cost = (total_tokens / 1000) * cost_per_1k print(f"₹{cost:.2f}") # ₹0.28 print(7 // 2) # 3 — floor division, discards the remainder print(7 % 2) # 1 — modulo, the remainder itself print(2 ** 10) # 1024 — exponent ``` `%` is genuinely useful: `if i % 100 == 0:` inside a loop is how you print progress every hundredth item without flooding your terminal. Comparison and logic: ```python is_valid = 0.0 <= temperature <= 2.0 # chained comparison — very Pythonic should_retry = (status_code >= 500) and (attempt < 3) use_default = system_prompt is None # 'is' for None, not '==' ``` Two rules that prevent real bugs. `=` assigns; `==` compares. And use `is None`, never `== None` — `is` checks identity, which is what you actually mean. **f-strings** are the modern way to build text, and you will use them constantly for prompts: ```python topic = "photosynthesis" level = "class 8" prompt = f"Explain {topic} to a {level} student in under 100 words." ``` ##### Conditional statements ```python def classify_prompt_length(tokens: int) -> str: if tokens > 100_000: return "too long — needs chunking" elif tokens > 8_000: return "long — use a large-context model" elif tokens > 0: return "fine" else: return "empty prompt" print(classify_prompt_length(12_000)) # long — use a large-context model ``` Python uses **indentation**, not braces, to define blocks. Four spaces, consistently. This is not a style preference — inconsistent indentation is a syntax error. Conditions check *truthiness*, not just `True`/`False`. Empty things are falsy: ```python chunks = [] if not chunks: print("Nothing retrieved — falling back to the base model.") ``` Empty string, empty list, empty dict, `0`, and `None` are all falsy. Everything else is truthy. This makes guard clauses very clean. ##### Loops **`for`** iterates over a sequence. This is the loop you will use 90% of the time. ```python documents = ["policy.pdf", "faq.md", "handbook.docx"] for doc in documents: print(f"Indexing {doc}...") # When you need the position too: for i, doc in enumerate(documents, start=1): print(f"{i}. {doc}") # When you need a count: for attempt in range(3): print(f"Attempt {attempt + 1} of 3") ``` **`while`** repeats until a condition becomes false. This is the loop that burned the Pune startup. ```python import time max_attempts = 5 attempt = 0 success = False while attempt < max_attempts and not success: attempt += 1 # ← the loop variable MUST change print(f"Calling API, attempt {attempt}") success = try_api_call() if not success: time.sleep(2 ** attempt) # exponential backoff: 2s, 4s, 8s... if not success: print("Gave up after 5 attempts.") ``` **The rule: every `while` loop needs something inside it that can make the condition false.** Point at that line before you run the code. If you cannot point at it, you have an infinite loop. `break` exits a loop early; `continue` skips to the next iteration: ```python for chunk in chunks: if not chunk.strip(): continue # skip blank chunks if budget_exceeded(): print("Budget cap hit — stopping.") break process(chunk) ``` ##### Functions and scope A function is a named, reusable block of code. Functions are how you stop copy-pasting. ```python def estimate_cost(text: str, price_per_1k_tokens: float = 0.15, chars_per_token: int = 4) -> float: """Rough cost estimate in ₹ for sending `text` to an LLM. Args: text: The prompt or document content. price_per_1k_tokens: Model price per 1,000 tokens. chars_per_token: Rough English approximation. Returns: Estimated cost in rupees. """ tokens = len(text) / chars_per_token return (tokens / 1000) * price_per_1k_tokens doc = "..." * 5000 print(f"₹{estimate_cost(doc):.2f}") print(f"₹{estimate_cost(doc, price_per_1k_tokens=2.50):.2f}") # keyword argument ``` Three things in that definition are habits worth forming immediately: - **Type hints** (`text: str`, `-> float`). Python does not enforce them, but your editor uses them to catch mistakes and your future collaborators use them to understand your intent. - **Default arguments** make functions flexible without demanding every caller supply every value. - **A docstring** in triple quotes. Three lines now saves twenty minutes later. **Scope** is which names are visible where: ```python model = "gpt-4o-mini" # global — visible everywhere def run(): attempts = 3 # local — exists only inside run() print(model) # can READ the global print(attempts) run() # print(attempts) # NameError — attempts doesn't exist out here ``` Variables created inside a function are local and vanish when it returns. This is a feature: it means a function cannot accidentally clobber something elsewhere in your program. **One dangerous default to know now:** never use a mutable object as a default argument. ```python def add_message(msg, history=[]): # BUG — the list is created ONCE history.append(msg) return history print(add_message("hi")) # ['hi'] print(add_message("bye")) # ['hi', 'bye'] ← surprise! def add_message(msg, history=None): # correct if history is None: history = [] history.append(msg) return history ``` ##### Virtual environments and pip This is the unglamorous topic that separates people whose code runs on other machines from people whose code does not. **The problem:** Project A needs `langchain==0.1.0`. Project B needs `langchain==0.3.5`. Install both globally and one of them breaks. Multiply by fifty packages. **The fix:** a virtual environment — a private, isolated Python installation per project. ```bash # 1. Create the project folder mkdir genai-day1 && cd genai-day1 # 2. Create a virtual environment named .venv python3 -m venv .venv # 3. Activate it source .venv/bin/activate # macOS / Linux # .venv\Scripts\activate # Windows PowerShell # Your prompt now shows (.venv) — you are inside the environment. # 4. Install packages — they go into .venv, not your system Python pip install openai python-dotenv # 5. Record exactly what you installed pip freeze > requirements.txt # 6. Leave the environment when done deactivate ``` Anyone who clones your project runs `python3 -m venv .venv`, activates it, and `pip install -r requirements.txt` — and gets your exact setup. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["System Python 3.11"] --> B[".venv for RAG chatbot
langchain 0.3.5
chromadb 0.5.0"] A --> C[".venv for fine-tune project
transformers 4.44
torch 2.4"] A --> D[".venv for API service
fastapi 0.115
openai 1.51"] B -.->|"isolated"| E["No version conflicts
between projects"] C -.-> E D -.-> E ``` Add `.venv/` to your `.gitignore`. Commit `requirements.txt`, never the environment folder itself — it is hundreds of megabytes and machine-specific. ##### Common mistakes - **Mixing tabs and spaces** for indentation. Configure your editor to insert 4 spaces on Tab. - **`=` where you meant `==`** inside an `if`. - **A `while` loop whose condition can never change** — the ₹2.8 lakh bug. - **Modifying a list while iterating over it.** Build a new list instead. - **Mutable default arguments** (`def f(x, items=[])`). - **`== None` instead of `is None`.** - **Working without a virtual environment**, then discovering your project only runs on your laptop. - **Committing `.venv/` to Git.** - **Single-letter variable names** everywhere except short loop counters. - **Ignoring the traceback.** Read the *last* line first — it names the error — then find the line number in your file. - **`input()` returns a string.** `input("Age: ") + 1` raises a TypeError; wrap it in `int()`. ##### Hands-on: build the reflexes Your practical task is small on purpose: install Python 3.11+, create a virtual environment, and write a script with a function that checks whether a number is prime using a loop. It touches everything from today — environment setup, a function, a loop, a conditional, a return value. The efficient version only tests divisors up to the square root; work out why that is enough, because reasoning about *why* a loop can stop early is the same muscle that keeps you from writing infinite ones. The mini project — a command-line budget calculator using functions and dictionaries — is your first taste of program *structure*. Resist writing it as one long block. Write `get_income()`, `get_expenses()`, `calculate_savings(income, expenses)`, and `print_breakdown(expenses)`. Four small functions you can test individually beat one forty-line script you can only test by running the whole thing. The assignment's five programs — temperature converter, FizzBuzz, factorial, palindrome checker, calculator — are deliberately classic. Do them, and push them to GitHub with a README listing what each one does. That repository is the first brick in a portfolio, and Day 45 of this course will care very much that it exists. ##### Key takeaways - **Python owns AI** because of readability plus a twenty-year ecosystem; every LLM SDK, vector database, and framework you will touch speaks it. - **Variables, operators, conditionals, and loops** are the whole toolkit — and a nested `dict` containing a `list` of `dict`s is literally the shape of an LLM API request. - **Every `while` loop needs a line inside it that can end the loop.** Point at that line before you run. - **Functions with type hints, default arguments, and docstrings** turn scripts into code other people can use — including future you. - **Always use a virtual environment** and commit `requirements.txt`, never `.venv/`. This is the difference between code that runs anywhere and code that runs on your laptop.
practical_task_reference: Install Python 3.11+, create a virtual environment, and write a script that takes a number and prints whether it is prime, using a loop and a function.
mini_project_reference: Build a command-line 'AI budget calculator' that asks for monthly income and expenses, then prints savings, a warning if overspending, and a category breakdown using functions and dictionaries.
assignment_reference: Write five small programs: a temperature converter, a FizzBuzz solution, a factorial calculator, a palindrome checker, and a simple calculator. Push them to a GitHub repository.
